segments.text: A Hybrid U-Net and Vision Transformer Framework with Dimensionality Reduction for Automated Detection of Throat Cancer Metastasis Abstract-Ensuring the early and accurate detection of lymph node metastasis continues to underpin prognostication and treatment for throat cancer patients. Histopathological whole-slide images (WSIs) are manually analyzed by pathologists in the clinical practice; however, this process is labour-intensive and requires a significant amount of time, leading to a poor reproducibility, inter-observer variability, and delays/inconsistencies in diagnostics. Addressing these limitations, we propose a U-Net segmentation, Vision Transformer (ViT)-based feature extraction, t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE) for dimensionality reduction, and Random Forest classification driven hybrid deep learning framework for fully automated patient-level detection. U-Net module segment lymph node regions from multimodal scan (MRI and PET) which makes the localization of somatic lesions clearer. Features extracted from the ViT both represent high and low spatial frequency histological signatures and long range relations that are then mapped via t-SNE to minimize within-cluster distance while maximizing between cluster distances both locally and globally. This then results in robust discrimination between metastatic and non-metastatic lymph nodes with a Random Forest classifier. The proposed method is evaluated on a benchmark throat cancer imaging dataset experimentally, where the results show that the proposed method significantly outperforms the conventional CNN based baselines, and the transformer only baselines achieving 97.6%, 96.8% and 95.9% accuracy, sensitivity and specificity respectively. These findings demonstrate not only the framework's ability to provide accurate diagnostic information, but also its potential to decrease training burden on pathologists substantially. Conclusions: The proposed model is a clinically achievable next step in enabling early, reliable and accurate identification of metastatic nodes in the throat to help guide treatment and improve outcomes in patients. Keywords-Throat cancer, metastasis detection, U-Net, Vision Transformer, t-SNE, Random Forest, medical image analysis, lymph node classification, automated oncology diagnostics I Introduction Cancers of the larynx, hypopharynx and oropharynx, collectively labelled as throat malignancies, have high propensity to metastasize in cervical lymphatics, a phenomenon which is crucial for determining lymph node status and the management of such patients [1][2]. The identification of lymph node metastasis (LNM) is also clinically important, as it is directly related to tumor stage, treatment strategy, and the survival of patients [3][4]. Reach of traditional methods such as histopathological examination, MRI and pet imaging among subsite specific groups is time consuming [5][6]. Moreover, the metastatic lymph nodes may demonstrate low-profile and highly complex architectural features, which are not separable using conventional image analysis and thus again will require advanced computational approaches for identification and classification [7][8] Deep learning models have recently been trained to automate LNM [9][10] detection, with early results suggesting that these algorithms may be faster and provide better detection results than experts.

segments.text: With skip connections, U-Net is a standard for medical image segmentation, learning local features by an encoder-decoder [11][12]. Despite these advantages, U-Net has limitations in long range dependencies of image data, potentially hindering the detection of subtle metastatic signatures[13][14]. On the other hand, since intra-image downstream tasks could benefit from the ability of vision transformers (ViT) to model global context [15][16], we have a more complementary method of capturing fine-grained spatial correlations across the image. By combining U-Net with ViT, local and global features can be extracted at the same time, making it easier to identify metastasis [17][18]. For example, various dimensionality reduction approaches such as t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE) are utilized to make high-dimensional features more interpretable, such that a clearer visualization and the separability of metastatic v non-metastatic clusters can be achieved [19][20]. Although these individual approaches show great potential, studies that integrate segmentation, feature extraction, dimensionality reduction, and classification into a comprehensive framework for fully automated LNM detection are still scarce [21]. Previous studies either worked on segmentation [22] or classification [23], while the overall pipeline is necessary for clinical translation. In addition, the evaluation of these hybrid models over multimodal imaging datasets (for example, MRI images and PET scans) is still limited [24]. There is a need for coordinated approach combining U-Net, ViT, t-SNE, and strong classifier to reliably demonstrate and predict the lymph node metastasis at the patient level in throat cancer. In this proposed hybrid framework, we combined cutting-edge deep learning architectures with dimensionality reduction techniques into a stand-alone automated pipeline for LNM detection. Then by using U-Net for accurate segmentation and ViT for long-distance contextual feature extraction in addition to t-SNE for feature optimization and T-SNE to visualize features and use Random Forest classification, this system strived to improve the accuracy of diagnosis while maintaining a light workload for pathologists [1][2][25]. The generalizability, reliability, and clinical applicability of the framework will be experimentally evaluated on benchmark throat cancer imaging datasets. This paper makes the following major contributions: ●​ A hybrid U-Net, Vision Transformer, t-SNE and Random Forest framework to automatically detect lymph node metastatic status in throat cancer. ●​ Evaluation of the framework across multimodal imaging data (MRI and PET) to quantitatively assess robustness and generalizability. ●​ Proof of concept clinical value through decreasing diagnostic burden and facilitating prompt and accurate metastatic lymph node detection The remainder of the paper is organized as follows: In Section 2, we review related works, including previously proposed methods for automated LNM detection and their limitations. In Section 3, we describe the proposed work where U-Net, ViT, t-SNE and Random Forest are integrated into a single framework. The empirical study is presented in Section 4 on the

Compared with manual assessment, the integration of clinical lymph node evaluation with radiomic features achieved superior diagnostic accuracy and reduced occult nodal metastasis rates. This underscores the importance of selecting appropriate network architectures to balance segmentation accuracy and radiomics reliability for downstream predictive modeling. ​ 2.1 Research Gap​ While there have been remarkable developments in the automatic detection, segmentation, and classification of the tumors and lymph nodes in cancers of head and neck, some difficulties still persist. Though existing models have shown high accuracy on modelled datasets [1–21], real-world generalizability remains poor over multi-institutional imaging sources with variable modality, resolution, as well as patient anatomy. Scalability is limited by the need for large labelled datasets that are labour-intensive and expensive to curate [17–21], a requirement of many deep learning approaches, including U-Net variants [22,23] and attention-based networks [24,25]. Moreover, the majority of these investigations are predominantly single-modality CT or MRI or PET (Positron Emission Tomography) imaging- or histopathology-based or cover specific anatomical regions (e.g. brain) with a few exceptions, and comprehensive multi-modal imaging (CT & MRI & MRI & PET [16-18]) or combining the imaging feature with clinical [19] or histopathological features have been rare [20]. Predictions from extant approaches are also poorly interpretable and clinically translatable, which remains a problem in the context of misclassification of
segments.label: human

segments.text: early-stage metastases or small lymph nodes [2][12][14]. In addition, not only TATE [14], but also other biological heterogeneity factors, rarely incorporated into the predictive models, restrict their capability in simulating metastasis [15]. Therefore, a multilayered approach is needed, with a limited reliance on manual analysis, exploring robust, multimodal, and clinically interpretable frameworks to automatically detect, localize, and classify lymph node metastases with generalizability in diverse patient populations. III Methodology​ This paper proposes a novel hybrid deep-learning framework based on U-Net-based segmentation guided by Vision Transformer (ViT) feature extraction, dimension reduction using t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (t-SNE), and Random Forest classification for the automatic detection of lymph node (LN) metastasis. First, multimodal imaging data such as MRI and PET scans are preprocessed to standardize the intensity, denoise the image and enhance tissue contrast to ensure the same quality of input is fed into each step of the analysis [22]. This U-Net module captures lymph node areas with high spatial accuracy, ensuring accurate localization of tissues that may be metastatic [23]. ViT extracted features hold details of spatiotemporal histology but also long-range deployable dependencies that t-SNE optimize to both preserve the geometry of the structure while better space for separability in classification tasks [24]. Lastly, a patient level Random Forest classifier combines the reduced feature set to classify metastatic vs. non-metastatic lymph nodes, resulting in a robust and interpretable prediction. By leveraging recent advances in hybrid architectures for medical image analysis [25], this multi-stage pipeline improves detection performance and decrease computational cost via effective combination of segmentation, representation learning and ensemble classification strategies. segments.text: Image Data: The HECKTOR Challenge Dataset [22] (Head and Neck Tumor Segmentation Challenge) was chosen as the main imaging data source for this study. We have selected this dataset as it offers multimodal imaging, consisting of co-registered PET and CT scans that have been shown to be key modalities for accurate lymph node metastasis detection in head and neck cancers [20]. Due to the provision of continuous annotations for main tumors and lymph nodes, this dataset is excellent for the formation of segmentation and categorization models. In contrast to smaller, localized institutional datasets that are often characterized by poor generalizability and convenient sampling bias, the HECKTOR dataset collects cases from multiple distinct cancer centers to increase diversity with respect to the patient population, tumor stages, and imaging conditions. This diversity enables evaluation of the proposed model in more clinically relevant situations. Secondly, the dataset has been used in several benchmarking challenges, confirming its acceptability and usability in the field of medical image research. Also, the reason for selecting this dataset is because it is consistent with the objective of the study to design a hybrid framework using multimodal imaging features and hence provide a strong ground to evaluate the proposed method. HECKTOR: Acquired for approximately 325 patients with head and neck squamous cell carcinoma of PET-CT images paired with simple ground truth annotations for TL (gross tumor volume) and nodes in each case. To make sure an accurate assessment of model performance can be measured, this data collection was separated into 70% for training (228 cases), 15% for validation (49 cases) and 15% for independent testing (48 cases) for this research. As far as imaging volumes go, they are provided in normalized size which means isotropic voxel size and harmonized protocols for acquisition that allows standard pre-processing and scanner-induced variability [8]. The scans of all patients have been labelled by experienced radiologists to generate gold-standard labels with the required quality for supervised learning. In addition, this dataset not only provides imaging data, but also optional assessment of subject-level metadata such as patient age, sex and clinical tumor stage to facilitate robust exploration (and future development) of multimodal fusion of imaging and clinical features. It has a sizeable dataset such that we can train deep learning architectures while it is still reasonable to compare with the state-of-the-art models that were reported before it, and is part of the HECKTOR [5] challenge. Strong points of our study included, access to a novel dataset through which a rigorous protocol for subject eligibility can be applied which has great potential for reproducibility and integration with state of the art imaging methodologies used for head and neck cancers. 3.2 Data Cleaning and Standardization​ To ensure reliable learning from multimodal imaging data, preprocessing was performed to reduce noise and normalize intensity distributions. T-SNE projections, ROC curves, and confusion matrices are some ways of visualizing this information and all support the strong discriminative power of the model and classification performance robustness. The various components incorporated are not merely included but the ablation study shows that they all contribute meaningfully to the overall performance with the dimensionality reducing, ensemble classification and application of a transformer based model, integrated in a hybrid form achieving the best prediction accuracy and reliability. Together, these findings emphasize the clinical promise of the proposed volumetric approach for accurate and reproducible detection of lymph node metastasis in patients with throat cancer. VI Conclusion​ We developed a hybrid deep learning framework that combines the input of U-Net segmentation, Vision Transformer-based feature extraction, t-SNE dimensionality reduction and Random Forest classification to perform automated detection of lymph node metastasis for throat cancer. This model overcomes the limitations of manual analysis including inter-observer variability and time-consuming processes. Using a benchmark data set for evaluation, we can show that our framework can accomplish 97.6%, 96.8%, and 95.9% accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity, respectively, far exceeding the standard CNN and transformer-only models. T-SNE plots, ROC curves and confusion matrices confirmed its excellent discriminative power, while ablation studies illustrated the contribution of each component. The high F1-score of 96.3% also suggests low imbalance between classes performance. In summary, the findings show the feasibility and robustness of the model to appropriately clinical utilize fast and accurate identification of metastasis. We will extend our method to multimodal datasets, introduce explainable AI for interpretability and conduct multi-center clinical trials to validate generalizability in future work.
